docs.title: Manning/Patrol Compliance System
docs.text:
A compliance-grade system documenting that stewards are present and active during night operation, against a contractual requirement that:

  • Trains are manned at least 70% of their running time
  • Every station level is patrolled at least once per rolling 60 minutes

With a verifiable real-time and historical record.

Semester Project

5th Semester, BSc Software Engineering, AAU Copenhagen · Autumn 2026

docs.title: Data Handling
docs.text:
Synthetic Data Only

This product runs on synthetic steward identities for the whole semester. No personal data is transferred to AAU. Never commit anything Metro supplied — this repository is public.

docs.title: System Context
docs.text: The Manning/Patrol Compliance System documents steward presence and patrol activity in the Copenhagen Metro during night operation. It consists of three deployable components that communicate through versioned contracts.

docs.title: Android App (Steward Client)
docs.text:
Location: apps/android/ Stack: Expo SDK 57, React Native, TypeScript

The steward-facing mobile app that: - Scans BLE beacons to detect presence in station areas (concourse, platforms, trains) - Manages patrol sessions (start/stop) - Posts connection/disconnection events to the backend - Receives real-time alerts via SSE

docs.title: Backend API
docs.text:
Location: services/api/ Stack: Python 3.13, FastAPI, SQLModel, PostgreSQL

The central service that: - Ingests positioning and patrol events (append-only event store) - Computes compliance metrics (manning %, patrol coverage) - Serves the web dashboard via SSE - Exposes versioned REST APIs defined in contracts/

docs.title: Web Dashboard
docs.text:
Location: apps/web/ Stack: Vite, React 19, TypeScript

The control-room dashboard that: - Shows real-time compliance status (trains manned ≥ 70%, stations patrolled hourly) - Displays historical records and overdue/at-risk stations - Consumes live updates via Server-Sent Events (SSE)

docs.text: Decision ADR Summary Positioning Interface ADR-0004 Areas defined by beacons; Android is source of truth for timestamps Database ADR-0007 PostgreSQL for relational + JSONB flexibility Event Store ADR-0008 Append-only event store, no update/delete paths Real-time Updates ADR-0011 Server-Sent Events for one-way server→client push Hosting ADR-0005 Ucloud (AAU) as staging environment

docs.title: Compliance Rules
docs.text:
The system enforces two contractual requirements:

  1. Manning: Trains must be manned ≥ 70% of running time
  2. Patrol: Every station level (concourse, platform) must be patrolled at least once per rolling 60 minutes

Coverage is computed from the append-only event store, with late-arriving reports handled per ADR-0009.

docs.title: Status Legend
docs.text:
• Proposed — decision is suggested, not yet ratified
  • Accepted — decision is ratified and in effect
  • Superseded — replaced by a newer ADR (link in the ADR itself)

docs.title: Creating a New ADR
docs.text:
1. Copy the next sequential number (e.g., 0012-my-decision.md)
  2. Follow the structure defined in ADR-0001:
  3. Status, Date, Deciders, Related backlog items
  4. Context — what is the issue?
  5. Decision — what was decided?
  6. Consequences — positive and negative impacts
  7. Alternatives considered — what else was evaluated?
  8. Notes — open questions, references
  9. Only the Status field may be changed after creation
  10. Add the new ADR to the navigation in docs/mkdocs.yml

docs.title: ADR 0001. Should architectural decisions be documented using ADRs?
docs.text:
Status. Proposed

Date. 2026-09-18

Deciders. Marcus Eckstrøm, Peter Rasmussen & Tue Elhegn, Team 3

Related backlog items. None

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
During the development of the system, key architectural decisions will be made that affect the design, implementation, and development of the project. These decisions often involve choosing between multiple alternatives based on requirements, constraints, and trade-offs.

Without a structured way of documenting these decisions, the reasoning behind them may be lost over time. This can make it difficult for team members and stakeholders to understand why a particular solution was chosen and which alternatives were considered.

Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) provide a consistent method for documenting architectural decisions and keeping track of the iterations of those.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Architectural Decision Records will be used throughout the project to document significant architectural decisions.

Each ADR will describe the context of the decision, the chosen solution, its consequences, and relevant alternatives that were considered. ADRs will be numbered sequentially and stored alongside the project documentation, allowing architectural decisions and their reasoning to be traced throughout the development process.

An ADR cannot be changed, so if a decision is changed, a new version will be made with links to the superseded ADR.

docs.title: Positive impact
docs.text:
• Provides a consistent structure for documenting architectural decisions.
  • Preserves the reasoning behind decisions and the alternatives that were considered.
  • Makes architectural decisions easier for team members and stakeholders to understand and review.
  • Provides a historical record that can support future changes to the system.

docs.title: Potential drawbacks
docs.text:
• Writing and maintaining ADRs requires additional development and documentation time.
  • ADRs can become outdated if architectural changes are made without updating or superseding the relevant records.
  • Determining which decisions are significant enough to require an ADR requires judgement from the development team.

docs.title: No formal decision documentation
docs.text: Architectural decisions could be discussed within the team and implemented without being formally recorded. This requires less documentation but makes it difficult to understand the reasoning behind previous decisions later in the project.

docs.title: General project documentation
docs.text: Architectural decisions could be documented as part of the general project documentation. This keeps documentation centralized but makes individual decisions and their consequences harder to identify and trace.

docs.title: Comments in source code
docs.text: Architectural reasoning could be documented close to the implementation through comments. This provides context directly within the code but is unsuitable for decisions that affect multiple components or concern the overall architecture.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: This ADR establishes the use of ADRs as the project's method for documenting architectural decisions. As the first ADR, it also defines the general structure that subsequent ADRs should follow. Future ADRs should use the same sections and numbering scheme to maintain consistency across the project.

docs.title: ADR 0011. Server-sent events for live compliance updates and steward alerts.
docs.text: Status. Proposed Date. 2026-10-19 Deciders. Asbjørn Gosvig, Jakob Michaelsen, Marcus Linde, Nichlas Christiansen, Rohan Atik, Ryan Zachariasen, team 8 Related backlog items. MET-B-007, MET-B-008, MET-B-009, MET-B-012, MET-B-013, MET-B-014, MET-B-015, MET-B-024

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Two clients need server-initiated updates. The web dashboard must show the current compliance status (trains manned >= 70% of running time and every station level patrolled hourly) without operations staff manually refreshing. The Android steward app must receive alerts and other relevant information — for example emerging compliance gaps or changes affecting their shift — pushed to them as they happen. In both cases the compliance state changes on the server side, when positioning and patrol events arrive in the event store, and the clients are pure consumers of that state: they never send data back on the same channel.

The backend is FastAPI, which supports streaming responses (text/event-stream) natively, and both clients — the browser-based dashboard and the Expo / React Native steward app — can consume an SSE stream. The traffic is one-way, server-to-client, over plain HTTP.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We will push live compliance updates and steward alerts from the API using Server-Sent Events (SSE): a long-lived HTTP response of type text/event-stream. Both the web dashboard and the Android steward app consume the same stream.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive impact

SSE matches the actual communication pattern: the server talks, clients listen. One mechanism serves both the dashboard and the steward app, instead of maintaining two push paths. It is plain HTTP, so it needs no protocol upgrade, works through existing proxies and load balancers, and is compatible with the API's ordinary authentication. Browser EventSource reconnects automatically after dropped connections, and the implementation surface is much smaller than a bidirectional protocol would be.

Potential drawbacks

On Android, mobile networks drop long-lived connections far more often than fixed lines, so the steward app must tolerate reconnect cycles and catch up on anything missed rather than silently losing alerts. The stream only works while the app is in the foreground, which is acceptable while a steward is on duty, but it is not a substitute for OS-level push if alerts must reach a closed app.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
WebSockets. Full-duplex and lower overhead per message, but both clients only consume updates, so bidirectionality buys nothing here. WebSockets add an upgrade handshake, a separate framing protocol, manual reconnection and heartbeat logic, and more connection state on the server. For a one-way push, that is complexity without benefit.

Client-side polling. The simplest option, but it forces a trade-off between latency and load: polling often enough for near-real-time compliance status and alerts means a stream of mostly wasted requests when nothing has changed, while SSE pushes exactly when the server state changes. No polling was also an acceptance criterion in MET-B-0002.

docs.title: ADR 0002. Is presence asserted by the system or confirmed by the steward?
docs.text:
Status. Accepted

Date. 2026-09-18

Deciders. Marcus Eckstrøm, Peter Rasmussen & Tue Elhegn, team 3

Related backlog items. MET-B-001, MET-B-004, MET-B-005, MET-B-007, MET-B-014, MET-B-024

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Our project involves taking a decision whether presence is asserted by the stewards manually or automatically by the system. Manual assertion: Under this approach, the steward manually determines and logs the steward’s presence at the relevant location or train by scanning a QR code at the location, or in the train. Automatic assertion: Under this approach, the system itself determines and logs the steward’s presence at the relevant location, or train based on Bluetooth beacon connection. Metroselskabet rejected the manual assertion based on the method not providing clear evidence of presence.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The presence of the stewards will be asserted and logged automatically by the system using Bluetooth beacons, as per request from Metro Service A/S.

Furthermore, this implies that if a steward is not connected to a Bluetooth beacon, they are not considered to be manning the station.

Platform checks may only require stewards to leave the train briefly during its 15–40 second stop. Requiring manual registration would add unnecessary work and reduce the time available for operational duties. Beacon-based detection provides automatic evidence of presence without requiring steward interaction.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive impact: - Reduces manual work and allows stewards to focus on manning trains and patrolling platforms and concourses. - Provides system-generated evidence of steward presence. - Eliminates missed registrations caused by stewards forgetting to scan a QR code.

Potential drawbacks: - Beacon detection confirms presence but cannot verify that the required patrol or task was actually performed. - Signal loss or inaccurate beacon detection may result in missing or incorrect presence records. - The system becomes dependent on the availability and reliability of the beacon infrastructure.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Facial recognition. Facial recognition is arguably the most precise and reliable technology. Cameras are already installed in every station, but the technology introduces a slew of privacy concerns and is very costly. GPS. GPS localization provides reliable and precise data, but the signal is lost underground. Working around this is not worth the cost compared to BLE beacons. Bluetooth triangulation/trilateration. Same method of tracking as GPS, but requires additional specialized hardware installed on stations/trains, making it costly.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: A key factor in this ADR is the contractual relation between Metro Service as contractor and Metroselskabet as client. Metroselskabet relies heavily on evidence of service from Metro Service and deemed it convenient for the stewards to scan arrival at a station but not doing the patrolling.

docs.title: ADR 0003. Which branching strategy should be used?
docs.text:
Status. Proposed

Date. 2026-09-21

Deciders. Sebastian Milo & Tue Elhegn, Team 3

Related backlog items. None

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The project requires a consistent branching strategy to support parallel development while keeping stable releases separate from ongoing work. GitFlow provides a structured approach with dedicated branches for development, features, releases, and fixes. This helps avoid unclear branching and a lot of merge conflicts.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
GitFlow will be used as the branching strategy.

The main branch will contain stable releases, while develop will be used to integrate ongoing development. Supporting branches will be used for specific purposes:

  • feature/* for new features.
  • release/* for preparing releases.
  • hotfix/* for urgent fixes to released versions.
  • bugfix/* for fixes to the development version.

Features and bug fixes are merged into develop. Releases and hotfixes are merged into both main and develop to keep the branches synchronized.

docs.title: Positive impact
docs.text:
• Provides a clear structure for development and releases.
  • Separates ongoing development from stable versions.
  • Supports parallel development of features and fixes.
  • Provides a clear release history through main.

docs.title: Potential drawbacks
docs.text:
• Introduces additional branches and merge operations.
  • Requires consistent use of the branching conventions.
  • Long-running branches may result in larger merge conflicts.
  • May introduce unnecessary overhead for a small project.

docs.title: GitHub Flow
docs.text: A simpler model based on main and short-lived feature branches. It reduces complexity but provides less separation between development and releases.

docs.title: Trunk-based development
docs.text: Changes are frequently integrated into a shared main branch. This reduces long-running branches but provides less isolation between ongoing development and stable releases.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: GitFlow was selected because its structured approach provides clear separation between ongoing development and stable releases while supporting parallel work within the teams.

docs.title: ADR POSITIONING INTERFACE CONTRACT.
docs.text:
Status. Accepted

Date. 2026-9-23

Deciders. Team 8, Asbjørn Gosvig, Jakob Michaelsen, Marcus Linde, Nichlas Christiansen, Rohan Atik, Ryan Zachariasen,

Related backlog items. B-002

Blocks: B-003, B-004, B-006, B-007, B-012, B-014, B-025

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The PBI demanded in the acceptance criteria that we create an observation-based design, where we don't poll constantly for updates. Furthermore, we have to manage connectivity so the server and the dashboard client know when the Android client is connected. This incentivizes us to manage which component will be the "source of truth" regarding timestamps and beacon connectivity. We also know that one station can have multiple beacons, e.g., Marmorkirken and Kongens Nytorv station have two beacons, both on separate platforms, and eventually all stations will have beacons on the concourse

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The main design is that areas are defined by beacons: trains, concourse and platforms which can then be connected to specific stations and trains

The Android client will send connection events to the server, which will propagate scenario state to connected clients via a WebSocket connection.

The Android client will send connection events as the source of origin to the server.

The backend will be the source of truth for data propagated to the dashboard.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
When we model the locations after beacons, it makes it easier to know exactly where the stewards are. The downside to this approach is it introduces a more complex database schema.

WebSockets introduce a layer of complexity and security measures in the implementation, but they reduce the network traffic, as we don't have to poll constantly for data via HTTP, as the acceptance criteria demanded.

Using the Android client as a source of origin for time gives the ability to have better timekeeping due to not being dependent on a constant connection to the backend for reliable data transfers. The drawback is the potential for time manipulation by the user of the Android device.

When we use the server as a source of truth, we avoid doing business logic in the dashboard's frontend. If the Android device disconnects, the backend may continue exposing the last known value unless the system handles stale data.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Using client as source of truth. We considered the server keeping track of time due to the potential of the user manipulating data, but due to the acceptance criteria and the lack of reliability on connection in the metro system, we opted not to.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: We assume that the stewards will have a working phone, and that it will not run out of power. An open question is we do not know the procedure of ownership for the Android devices.

docs.title: ADR 0005. Ucloud as cloud platform.
docs.text: Status. Proposed Date. 2026-09-23 Deciders. Peter Rasmussen, Sebastian Milo, team 3 Related backlog items. MET-b-004, MET-b-005, MET-b-012, MET-b-013, MET-b-020, MET-b-021, MET-b-023, MET-b-025

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Creating a simulation for case-b-manning-patrol requires a common platform to extensively test and run the application(s), in an environment as close to production as possible. It serves as a baseline from which the teams can build from and against. Even if the application(s) are not deployed directly into Metro Service systems, the teams still have functioning software, emulating a real-world software environment. Ucloud is a new hosting service provided by AAU, which provides a secure and safe environment, targeting students for easy collaboration and high accessibility. The first choice was STRATO, but it has been deprecated for student use^1.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We will host our application(s) on AAU Ucloud servers as a safe staging environment, with the possibility to expand the pipeline to deployment in the future.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Pros Ucloud is accessible for all students and the recommended platform from CLAAUDIA support^1. It removes some liability in the case of data privacy from the student onto AAU, compared to external/corporate cloud services.

Cons Ucloud is a new and unknown service to all the teams, which will incur an additional on-boarding cost setting it up correctly. This cost is entirely unknown, so planning resources for it is guess work in the beginning. As with any early decision, this commits us in the long run and can provide costly to reverse later in the process.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
AWS/Azure/Cloudfire - Large cloud hyperscale platforms. Although close to production-like environment, these options are unnecessary for the scope and requirements for case-b-manning-patrol. Could turn costly if freemium plan provides inadequate features/tools.

Vercel/Heroku/Render - PaaS application platforms. Closer to the scope of the project compared to the large providers, but working with 'in-house' hosting from Ucloud seems more suitable for a student project.

STRATO - The previous AAU/CLAAUDIA service, now restricted to researchers and not students.

Localhost. Not hosting online lowers the environment fidelity, not emulating a real world scenario of software development/scenario.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: 1. Screenshot from CLAAUDIA support in commit history. Also https://hpc.aau.dk/ outlining the different access privileges of CLAAUDIA services.

docs.title: ADR POSITIONING INTERFACE CONTRACT.
docs.text:
Status. Proposed

Date. 2026-10-05

Deciders. Team 8, Asbjørn Gosvig, Jakob Michaelsen, Marcus Linde, Nichlas Christiansen, Rohan Atik, Ryan Zachariasen,

Related backlog items. MET-B-004

Blocks B-005, B-006, B-007

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
We assume that a beacon connection is not a connection in the Bluetooth sense. The steward's Android device passively receives advertising packets, and the connection exists for as long as packets keep arriving. Packets are sometimes missed especially when the device is in the pocket of a steward. Without a tolerance, a single stay would split into several shorter records each time the signal dropped, and any piece shorter than x would be discarded, so work actually carried out would go unrecorded.

The gap is therfore bound from two sides:

Lower bound The gap must exceed the interruptions that occur while the steward remains in place, so that ordinary packet loss and scan intervals do not split a record.

Upper bound The gap must be shorter than the briefest genuine absence we want the system to register. This could be a steward stepping of the train onto the platform, or going up the escalator from the platform to the concourse.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We will treat a beacon as lost only after 10 seconds without an observation. A beacon observed again within 10 seconds continues the open record.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
What becomes easier Brief losses of signal no longer fragment records, so a steward who stays in one area produces one record.

What becomes harder

An absence of less than 10 seconds is not detected.

An interruption longer than 10 seconds while the steward remains in place still splits the record.

The gap constrains the choice of x. If x is shorter than or equal to the gap, two isolated observations could complete a record consisting mostly of gap time. If x is chosen to be less that the gap, we must choose a new one.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
A tolerated gap of 20 seconds

This is the current default in the Estimote SDK. It was rejected because it reaches the upper bound, a steward who leaves a stopped train for about 20 seconds to check the platform would not be registered as having left the train.

A tolerated gap of 5 seconds

This would register short absences more precisely. It was rejected because it lies close to the interval between observations that Android can produce

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Industry practice places the value between 10 and 20 seconds:

The Android Beacon Library (AltBeacon) uses a default tolerated gap of 10 seconds https://github.com/AltBeacon/android-beacon-library/blob/aca69f9bc7f3526032e6e5fcc3593a3259c7d2d4/lib/src/main/java/org/altbeacon/beacon/BeaconManager.java#L195-L198

Estimote raised its default from 10 to 20 seconds https://github.com/Estimote/Android-SDK/blob/1f4ef1c1255b2fd4b09c4e80780d342cbb1b09ab/CHANGELOG.md?plain=1#L192-L197

According to estimote 10 seconds can be too short of a gap when scanning is not reliable. We accept that risk because we scan continuously in the foreground and because the upper bound rules out 20 seconds.

docs.title: ADR 0007. PostgreSQL as database
docs.text:
Status. Proposed

Date. 2026-10-07

Deciders. Peter Rasmussen, Tue Elhegn, Maya Lauritsen, Markus Jørgensen, Jacob Jensen, Signe Jensen, Patrick Hallberg, Victor Zacho, team 3, team 2

Related backlog items. MET-B-004, MET-B-013, MET-B-018, MET-B-019, MET-B-020, MET-B-021, MET-B-023, MET-B-024

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The project uses relational data, including reference data such as stations and patrol areas, alongside dynamic data in the form of steward connection and disconnection events. The reference data is used to associate events with locations in the metro network. PostgreSQL supports these relational relationships while also providing JSON and JSONB column types, allowing event payloads to be stored as flexible documents within a relational database.

The database systems course teaches PostgreSQL, giving the team existing experience with the technology. PostgreSQL also satisfies the database requirements identified by the project. Other database systems, including more specialized solutions such as EventStoreDB, were considered, but their additional technological overhead was deemed unnecessary.

This ADR is related to PBI MET-B-020, which does not explicitly require implementation yet. However, the teams prioritized making the database decision now, as Sprint 2 is focused on designing the database.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: PostgreSQL is selected as the database for the backend.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
The decision provides developers with a defined database technology and a concrete platform to build and test against. It also allows testing to progress from unit testing towards integration testing against the selected database.

Choosing PostgreSQL introduces further technical decisions regarding database drivers, ORMs, deployment, and containerization. These decisions will need to be addressed as development progresses.

The choice also means that the project's append-only event requirements will be handled within PostgreSQL rather than through a specialized event-store database.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
EventStoreDB. A specialized database system that is well suited to the append-only event requirement. However, it was considered excessive for the project's needs, given the additional technological overhead it would introduce.

Other SQL databases. Other relational database systems could satisfy the project's requirements. No project-specific reason strongly favored one over another. PostgreSQL was the natural choice given the team's existing experience with it through the database systems course.

docs.title: ADR 0008. Append-only Eventstore decision.
docs.text: Status. Proposed Date. 2026-10-09 Deciders. Peter Rasmussen, Tue Elhegn, team 3 Related backlog items. MET-B-020

docs.title: Context
docs.text: PBI MET-B-020 suggests append-only storage for the records in the database, as these are used for the compliance reports that Metro Service presents to Metro Selskabet, as evidence of manning requirements. This means we develop a database relation that has no code path for changes and only appends new events, without the possibility of updating or deleting records, in the event store. This will be treated as a source of truth for all parties.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We will implement and enforce an append only event store with no code path updating or deleting events.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive impact An append-only event store is a well documented concept in software engineering and is fitting for this case in particular. It is a simple solution to a critical problem.

Potential drawbacks Having this append-only event store be source of truth and compliance-crucial, requires strict enforcement and leverage of security protocols. This decision might complicate the development further down the line, as an append-only structure is limiting what we can do with the data in the backend.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: Audit log versioning. Was considered, but as the PBI already suggested append-only, it was reasonable to choose that solution.

docs.title: ADR 0009. An observation, which arrives after the shift it belongs to has been reported, is handled by a stated rule, rather than silently accepted
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 2026-10-16

Deciders: Sebastian Juel Milo, Héðinn Snær Arnarson, Group 3

Related backlog items: MET-B-006

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A handheld that reconnects after a period underground will deliver observation late. Without this rule compliance percentages are quietly wrong.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Based on an answer from Metro in August 2026, if an observation arrives late, a report will be reissued. The report is therefore a versioned artefact rather than a file produced once. A reissue supersedes the earlier version, however the earlier version remains retrievable.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Based on the work on the append-only event store (0008-append-only-event-store-decision.md) which stores both the handheld timestamp and the server timestamp, we already have the data required to version reports, therefore the acceptance criteria from MET-B-006: "An observation arriving out of order is placed by its observation timestamp" is trivially solved.

Positive Impact: - If a steward disconnects from a station, but reconnects 5 minutes after the patrol countdown will be based on when he leaves the station and not when he arrives.

Potential drawbacks: - Generation of the reports will be more complex, but remains a seperate issue.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text: No alternatives considered as this was a requirement coming straight from Metroservice.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: This ADR only describes how the data will be stored to later generate the report and does not consider how to actually generate a report.

docs.title: ADR 0010. Patrol completion: rolling hour and independent levels.
docs.text: Status. Proposed Date. 2026-10-16 Deciders. Asbjørn Gosvig, Jakob Michaelsen, Marcus Linde, Nichlas Christiansen, Rohan Atik, Ryan Zachariasen, team 8 Related backlog items. MET-B-007, MET-B-008, MET-B-009, MET-B-012, MET-B-013, MET-B-014, MET-B-015, MET-B-024

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The requirement states that every station level is patrolled hourly. When determining how to track when an area was last manned there are different ways of implementing it, and two questions must be answered:

  1. What does "hourly" mean? A level could be checked against fixed wall-clock hours (e.g. 14:00–14:59, a patrol per bucket), or against a rolling 60-minute window: a level is compliant at a given moment if there is evidence of coverage at some point in the last hour.
  2. Are the levels independent? A station's levels (concourse and platform) are physically very close to each other, often only a staircase apart, and a steward visiting one will usually visit the other soon after. There is therefore also the question of their independence: should a visit to one level count for the station as a whole, or must each level show coverage on its own?

The acceptance criteria of the related backlog items already speak of each level separately, which points towards independent evaluation.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
We use a rolling hour for determining whether something is manned or not: a level is compliant at time t if patrol role is fuldfilled for that level within the last 60 minutes.

The two levels are computed independently.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive impact

  • Faithful to the plain reading of "patrolled hourly": at any moment, the last hour must contain a patrol. There is no way for two patrols almost two hours apart to both count.
  • Simple to compute. Compliance at time t is a lookup for records in [t − 60 min, t]. No mutable "patrol completed" state has to be maintained; the append-only event store remains the single source of truth and compliance is derived from it.
  • Independence matches the acceptance criteria and prevents one level from masking a gap on the other.

Potential drawbacks

  • Compliance decays with time, not only with events: a level can go from compliant to non-compliant without any new record arriving, as an older patrol slides out of the window. Dashboards and alerts must therefore re-evaluate on a timer, not only on ingestion.

  • Any single observation counts as coverage. It documents presence within the hour, not that a full patrol was performed — a limitation inherited from beacon-based presence assertion (ADR 0002).

  • Independent levels add patrol work: a steward assigned to train manning may often cover the platform frequently, and in many cases then have to also return to the concourse solely to satisfy its patrol requirement.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
Fixed wall-clock hours. Treat each [hh:00, hh:59] bucket as an hour and require a patrol in every bucket. Rejected: patrols at 14:01 and 15:59 leave a gap of almost two hours yet both buckets pass, which contradicts the intent of hourly patrolling. The rolling window is the stricter reading.

One area per station. Treat the concourse and platform as a single area so that a visit to either covers the station. Rejected: the requirement applies to every level, and a steward can serve the platform without ever reaching the concourse. The acceptance criteria already treat the levels separately.

Completion-based cadence. Declare a patrol complete when the steward leaves the level (after the tolerated gap, ADR 0006) and require the next patrol within 60 minutes of that completion. Rejected: it depends on reliably detecting an exit, which is weaker than detecting presence, and it requires mutable per-level state that the append-only event store deliberately does not provide.

docs.title: Android App
docs.text:
Steward-facing Android app built with Expo SDK 57, React Native, and strict TypeScript.

Location: apps/android/

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Node.js 20 or 22
  • npm >= 11.4.2
  • Expo Go app (for quick testing) or Android emulator

docs.title: Running Locally
docs.text:
cd apps/android
npm install
EXPO_PUBLIC_API_URL=http://<your-lan-ip>:8000 npx expo start

From the Expo developer menu, open the app in: - Expo Go (quickest, no build needed) - Android emulator - Development build on a physical device (needed for BLE beacon scanning)

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Description npm run start expo start npm run android expo start --android (emulator) npm run ios expo start --ios (simulator) npm run web expo start --web npm run lint expo lint npx tsc --noEmit TypeScript type check npm test Vitest tests

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text:
apps/android/src/
├── app/                         # expo-router file-based routes
│   ├── index.tsx                # Patrol session slider demo
│   └── beacon.tsx               # Mock beacon scanner demo
├── components/                  # UI building blocks

├── state/                       # Pure reducers
├── types/                       # Domain types and initial states

docs.title: Beacon Scanning
docs.text:
The app receives beacon connect/disconnect events shaped as ConnectionEvent from contracts/positioning-ingestion/v2:

{
  android_id: string,
  beacon_id: string,
  event: "connect" | "disconnect",
  timestamp: string
}

Everything that produces these events implements the BeaconScanner interface (src/services/beacon/scanner.ts).

docs.title: Mock vs Real Scanning
docs.text:
• MockBeaconScanner — simulates a steward walking past beacon IDs from the backend fixtures. No Bluetooth needed; runs in Expo Go and emulator.
  • Real BLE scanning — same interface, requires a development build on a physical device.

Not yet wired up

Forwarding events to the backend (POST /api/v2/connection/connect and /api/v2/connection/disconnect) is not implemented yet.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Hooks take side effects as parameters — usePatrolSession receives the start/stop requests, useBeaconScanner receives the scanner. Swap the implementation, not the hook.
  • Reducers are pure — no requests, timers, or other side effects inside.
  • The phone is the source of truth for event time (see ADR-0004).

docs.text:
SDK 57

Check the versioned Expo docs before writing Expo-specific code. APIs change between versions.

docs.text:
cd services/api
uv sync                          # install dependencies
docker compose up -d             # start PostgreSQL (port 5432)
cp .env-example .env             # set DATABASE_URL
uv run alembic upgrade head      # apply migrations
uv run dev                       # start with auto-reload on :8000

The .env file should contain: 

DATABASE_URL=postgresql+asyncpg://metro:admin@localhost:5432/metro

docs.title: Database
docs.text:
The backend uses PostgreSQL through SQLModel and the async asyncpg driver.

  • Migrations: Alembic manages the schema. Always apply migrations before starting the server: 

    uv run alembic upgrade head

  • Creating a migration after changing a model: 

    uv run alembic revision --autogenerate -m "describe the change"
uv run alembic upgrade head
uv run alembic check         # verify models and migrations agree

  • Seeding: Load the fixture event timeline: 

    uv run python -m src.scripts.seed

  • Resetting: Drop all tables and re-apply migrations: 

    uv run reset-db

Migration gotcha

create_all runs on server startup. If you start the server before applying migrations, tables are created without Alembic's version record and alembic upgrade head will fail with "table already exists".

docs.title: Positioning Simulator
docs.text:
The API includes a simulator implementing the Positioning Interface contract (contracts/positioning-interface/v1/):

  • GET /observations — currently active area observations
  • GET /observation-events — all observation events
  • GET /ws/observation-events — WebSocket stream of events

Fixture: fixtures/fixture-events-v1.json — event timeline replayed by the simulator.

Run the simulator: 

uv run positioning-simulator

docs.text:
uv sync --locked                 # install locked dependencies
export DATABASE_URL=...          # set as environment variable (not .env)
uv run alembic upgrade head      # apply migrations

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
Versioned OpenAPI interfaces that define how components communicate. Other teams build against these contracts.

Location: contracts/

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
contracts/
├── README.md
└── api/
    ├── v1/                          # Initial versions
    │   ├── CHANGELOG.md
    │   ├── positioning-interface/   # Observation events (simulator)
    │   │   ├── README.md
    │   │   └── schema.json
    │   └── positioning-ingestion/   # Connection events from Android
    │       ├── README.md
    │       └── schema.json
    └── v2/                          # Current versions
        ├── CHANGELOG.md
        ├── positioning-interface/   # Dashboard SSE stream
        ├── positioning-ingestion/   # Patrol session + connection events
        ├── positioning-adjustment/  # Manual adjustments (draft)
        └── health/                  # Health check endpoints

docs.title: Versioning Rules
docs.text: Contracts are published and immutable — never edit a released version in place. Add a new version directory instead.

docs.title: When to create a new major version
docs.text:
If the update breaks the existing system (URL changes, endpoints removed, fields renamed):

  1. Create a new directory (e.g., v2/) and copy the latest schema from the old version
  2. Mark the old version as deprecated in its README.md and schema.json ("deprecated": true in OpenAPI)
  3. Document the sunset date in the old version's README.md and CHANGELOG.md
  4. Update the prefix throughout the repo so code and endpoint mounts point to the new contract

docs.title: When to bump minor version
docs.text:
If the change is only an addition (new optional fields or endpoints) and does not break the system:

  1. Update the info.version field in schema.json (e.g., v1.0.0 → v1.1.0)
  2. Document the change in the CHANGELOG.md of that version

docs.title: When to bump patch version
docs.text:
For bug fixes (typos, corrected examples):

  1. Update the info.version field in schema.json (e.g., v1.0.0 → v1.0.1)
  2. Document the fix in the CHANGELOG.md

docs.title: CHANGELOG.md
docs.text: Each versioned directory (v1/, v2/, etc.) must include a CHANGELOG.md documenting changes for that version.

docs.title: Backend Connection
docs.text:
The dashboard connects to the backend API for: - Real-time compliance status via Server-Sent Events (SSE) - Historical records and coverage data via REST

Configure the API URL in the environment or settings file.

docs.title: Development Notes
docs.text:
• The type check lives in npm run build (tsc -b). Never bypass it with vite build alone.
  • React Compiler is enabled — avoid manual useMemo/useCallback unless profiling shows a real need.
